title: Packaging, partners and a web address
lede: Clearly Canadian said advertising was not affordable for its niche brands.[^4] The record shows what it used instead: the bottle, retail partners, sampling and a web address printed on the package.[^8]

blocks.title: How Orbitz reached buyers
blocks.subtitle: What the sources document, by lever.
rows: Aimed at ages 12 to 17 or even college students, by AP’s account.[^1]

Marketing vice-president Jonathan Cronin said mass advertising did not suit the company’s niche products and was not affordable, so it sought attention through product placement and sampling, and through event marketing.[^4]
In Canada the campaign theme was “Defy Gravity. Get into Orbitz.”[^8]
A national in-store promotion with HMV Records, consumer sampling at Famous Players theatres and a three-year sponsorship agreement with Rollerblade Inc.[^8]

In Canada, sales began May 1, 1997 at accounts such as 7-Eleven, Shoppers Drug Mart and Famous Players cinemas. In April 1997 the drink was in convenience stores and supermarkets in the United States and New Zealand.[^8]
A 300 ml glass bottle that won the 1996 Glass Packaging Institute Clear Choice Award and the 1996 Mobius International Award. Four flavors at the Canadian launch.[^8]
The address of the Planet Orbitz site, www.orbitz.com, was displayed on all packaging. The site carried comics by the syndicated artist Dirk Van Stralen and a tour of an Orbiterium spaceship.[^8]
$1.09 for a 10.14-ounce bottle in Spokane in January 1997.[^2] A company-history reference says it cost as much as 50 percent more than regular sodas.[^13]

Atlantic Beverage Co. was the sole, exclusive distributor of Orbitz and Clearly Canadian beverages in the Washington region in April 1997.[^3] A company-history reference says Clearly Canadian bought back distribution rights in several key Mid-Atlantic states in June 1998.[^13]
blocks.source: Business Wire release of April 14, 1997 (a company statement),[^8] Strategy,[^4] and the other sources cited in each row.
